title: How a community sports club should write an about page
metaTitle: How a sports club should write about
excerpt: An about page should name the people who run the sessions and why a new member should care. Skip the origin story unless it changes the decision to join.
alt: An OPEN sign hanging in a shop window, with the word SHOP printed on the glass. A plain signal that someone is inside, which is the job of an about page.
caption: An OPEN sign in a shop window, with SHOP printed on the glass. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Who belongs on a club about page?
faqs.answer: Name the people a new member will meet: the coach of the trial, the junior coordinator, the welfare contact. Under each name, state the job, the qualification that matters, and the session they run. A line about passion fits every club and tells the reader nothing they can check.

faqs.question: When is a founding story worth telling?
faqs.answer: Tell it when it changes Tuesday. A late session that still exists for shift workers is a useful origin. A fond memory of 1978 with no consequence for the current offer can be one sentence, or a history note for people who already belong.

faqs.question: How long should the page be?
faqs.answer: Short enough to read on a phone outside the hall. A few coaches, a welfare line, one paragraph on who the club is for, and the link to membership or the schedule is a complete page. A timeline with twenty dates will be skipped.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A community sports club about page is proof that specific people stand behind the offer. Name who runs the sessions and why a member deciding whether to join should care. Skip the origin myth unless that story changes the decision to see membership or the schedule.

The page answers a human question. Who will be there on my first night, and are they responsible for the room. A chronology of the club's founding rarely answers it.

## Name the people who do the work

Start with the names a new person will meet. The head coach. The junior coordinator. The club captain who greets trials. The welfare contact, if the club has one. A photograph of each, taken in the place they actually work, beats a stock handshake. A short line under the name should say the job, the qualification that matters, and the session they are attached to.

"Coach of the Tuesday social, level 2, played here for six years" is a useful biography. "Passionate about growing the game" fits every coach in the sport and tells the reader nothing they can check. Specifics are the proof. Years are fine when they are true. Invented warmth is easy to smell.

Google's guidance on [people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) treats the question of who created something as part of trust. On a club site the "who" is the coaching and volunteer group, not a hidden author of the web page. Make that group visible. If a page about juniors has no named adult, a parent has a fair reason to hesitate. Trust, in that guidance, matters more than a pile of slogans. Show the person.

Keep the list current. A coach who left in the spring should not still be welcoming people in September. Stale names are a special kind of falsehood because the reader may meet the absence in person. Put the about page on the same review cycle as the schedule.

## Why this member should care

The second job of the page is relevance. A beginner cares that a named coach runs a session for new people, and that nobody is laughed off the court. A parent cares that juniors are supervised, that collection is organized, and that there is a person to call. A competitive player cares that the squad trains with a purpose and plays real fixtures.

Write a short block for each of those readers, or write one honest paragraph that names the mix you actually serve. Pretending the club is equally perfect for every reader produces a page that none of them can use. If you are a competitive club with a patient beginner hour, say both, and say they are different nights.

Connect the people to the decision you want. After the names, the page should still offer a way to see membership or the schedule. An about page that ends on a poem has forgotten why the visitor came. They were checking whether the offer has humans attached. Once that check passes, they need the door.

You can mention how the club behaves without a values poster. We put new players with a host for the first half hour. We publish the fees. We answer membership email within a few days, if that is a promise you keep. Behavior is stronger than a list of words like respect, excellence, and family. Anyone can typeset those words. Fewer clubs can describe the first half hour.

## When an origin story earns its place

An origin story earns a place when it changes the decision. The club was started so shift workers could train at 9 p.m., and that session still exists. The club shares a hall with two other sports, which is why the schedule looks the way it does. The club is attached to a school, and the public sessions are listed separately from school hours. Those facts help someone join.

A story about a founder who loved the sport in 1978, with no consequence for Tuesday, can live in a single sentence or on a history page for people who already belong. It should not lead. Leading with it tells a new person that the club is a memorial. Some clubs are proudly old. Age can be one line, next to the fact that new members are how the club continues. The line has to include the welcome, or the age reads as a gate.

Anniversaries are the same. A centenary is a pleasant fact. It is a weak headline for a person choosing a weeknight. Put the centenary in the footer of the story, after the coaches and the way in.

If you do tell a longer story, tell it in concrete scenes. The first hired hour in a cold hall. The decision to open a junior section after members had children. Avoid a cinematic voice. The reader is a neighbor, and they can visit. Write as if they might.

## Committees, volunteers, and the welfare line

Many clubs are run by volunteers, and that is a strength when you explain it. Say that the committee is elected, what it is responsible for, and that coaching questions go to the coach, while fees questions go to the treasurer. A new member who emails the wrong person and hears nothing concludes the club is asleep. The about page can prevent that by naming the route.

List roles rather than a novel about governance. Chair, secretary, treasurer, welfare, junior coordinator. An email or a form for each, or one form that routes, if you will truly route it. Publish the welfare contact in plain text. Safety information that is only inside a PDF will be skipped by the parent who is skimming on a phone.

Volunteer-run does not mean amateur in the careless sense. If coaches are qualified, say the qualification. If the club is affiliated to a governing body, say which one, because that affiliation is a fact a careful parent looks up. Affiliation is proof. A paragraph about passion is not.

Photographs of volunteers should look like the club. A committee standing in the car park in club tops is honest. A rented boardroom is a different organization. Use pictures you have rights to, and avoid putting children's faces on a governance page. The junior coach can be shown. The children belong on the junior session page, with consent.

## What to leave off this page

Leave off the trophy cabinet as the main event. A sentence and a link to a season review is enough for pride. Leave off sponsor logos as the visual lead. Leave off a timeline with twenty dates nobody will read. Nielsen Norman Group notes, in its piece on [how long people stay on pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/), that visitors often leave within 10 to 20 seconds and read only about a quarter of the text. An about page that begins in 1978 spends the quarter on the wrong years.

Leave off quotes you cannot stand behind. A testimonial from "Sarah, local mum" with no permission and no specificity is filler. If a member has said something true and is happy to be named, one quote under the relevant coach is plenty. Do not invent one to fill a layout. Hanabi will not invent client quotes, and a club should not invent member quotes either.

Facilities deserve one concrete line if they change the decision to travel. Two courts and a viewing balcony. A river launch with a long walk from the car park. Lights until 10 p.m. Skip the architectural essay. The person is checking whether the place can host the session you described, and whether they can picture arrival.

Leave the page shorter than you think. Four coaches, one welfare line, one paragraph on who the club is for, and the link to membership or the schedule. That page can be read on a phone outside the hall. A history essay cannot.

## Make the heading match the proof

The visible title of the page should say what the page is. "People" or "Coaches and contacts" is clearer than "Our story" when the content is names and roles. Google's title guidance favors a descriptive title that matches the main heading on the page. If the heading says "Our story" and the useful content is a list of coaches, the title is doing decorative work and the list is doing the real work. Promote the list.

Use the club's name once, in the title or beside it. Repeating the name in every subheading makes the page sound like a template. The reader is already on your site.

Write bios in the club's voice. Short sentences. Concrete nouns. The same voice as the homepage. If the homepage sounds like a coach and the about page sounds like a grant application, the visitor feels two organizations. Pick the coach.

## From names to a single season, clearly told

Once people can see who runs the room, some of them want a fuller account of a decision the club made: opening the beginner course, fixing the timetable, rebuilding a junior section. A single proof page can show the constraint, the choice, and people playing, then point back to membership or the schedule. That is the job of [proof pages for a community sports club](/blog/proof-pages-for-a-community-sports-club).

Club sites with a clear human face sit with [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). Read them for whether you can tell who does the work.
